e.t: Belshazzar is a personal name, referring to the Babylonian king named in the book of Daniel. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs seven times, all in Daniel, from Daniel 5:1 through Daniel 7:1. It identifies the same person across these references rather than describing a quality, action, or object. The name is rendered “Belshazzar,” and its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word is a place name, referring to Baale in Judah. It is rendered “Baale” and “Judah,” identifying the location as Baale associated with the territory or people of Judah rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 2 Samuel 6:2. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary function is geographic: it names a particular place connected with Judah.

This Hebrew verb expresses the action of making something “polluted.” It describes a condition in which a person, object, or sacred matter is treated as contaminated or unfit. In the Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, including passages rendered “polluted” and contexts involving people, sacred things, and choices. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject. The word therefore focuses on the resulting polluted condition rather than merely on outward appearance.

Adar is the name of a month. In the Old Testament, it appears eight times, all in Esther, where it identifies the time of events and dates. The word itself functions as a month name rather than describing an action, person, or quality. Its occurrences span Esther 3:7 through Esther 9:21, including several references in the account of events occurring during Adar.

This word means “Gilonite,” identifying a person connected with or from a place called Giloh. It functions as a descriptive name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in 2 Samuel: once for Ahithophel and once for Eliam. The word itself supplies a place-based designation; the surrounding verse is needed to explain each person’s particular role in the narrative. Its repeated use shows that “Gilonite” identifies a recognized geographic or family connection.

This Hebrew word means “cut.” It expresses an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 31:22, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains the act of cutting. The word’s identity and its repeated English rendering support this basic meaning.

This Hebrew word describes a condition of calm or stillness, when disturbance has ceased and quiet remains. It can refer to outward calm, such as the settling of turmoil, or to silence and stillness. In the Old Testament, it occurs three times, with the approved renderings pointing to “calm” and “still.” Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew noun means “curtain.” It names a fabric covering or hanging partition rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 40:22, so its normal lexical range is represented by this single occurrence. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a curtain.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “branch,” referring to a woody growth extending from a tree or vine. It is used five times in the Old Testament, including descriptions of branches as visible plant material and as something associated with a vine’s usefulness. The word’s ordinary sense remains focused on a branch rather than the whole tree. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “mast,” functioning as a noun that names the upright support of a vessel. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, with its only recorded occurrence in Proverbs 23:34. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete rather than a broad description of a person, action, or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

The word refers to a “privy,” naming a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 21:14. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be described further without adding information. Its supported meaning remains simple and specific: a privy.

In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 15:18. The available scriptural connections place the name in relation to speech, giving, dwelling, and taking, but the surrounding verse text is not available here, so those connections do not establish a broader lexical meaning beyond the name itself.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes a strong desire for something, expressed as “covet” or “desired.” It can refer to wanting possessions, valuable things, or something regarded as desirable. Its 28 Old Testament occurrences show that the word can describe desire in both negative and positive settings, so the surrounding passage determines whether the desire is condemned or simply recognized. The word appears from Genesis through Micah, including descriptions of treasured or desirable things and warnings against coveting what belongs to another.

This Hebrew verb means “consume,” describing the action of using up or swallowing something. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Deuteronomy 28:38. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its single occurrence means this word has a narrow recorded range in the Hebrew Bible, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. The word is connected there with other terms describing what happens to the field and its produce.

This Hebrew word means “all.” It expresses the entirety of whatever it qualifies or describes, rather than a limited portion. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both in Ezekiel 16:4. The available record identifies it as a predicate, meaning it helps make an assertion about another word or element. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a divine name used to identify God. It refers to the God of Israel as the one addressed, spoken of, and associated with divine actions throughout the Old Testament. In the Hebrew corpus, it occurs 306 times across 296 verses, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its dominant meaning is “GOD,” and its repeated use marks a personal designation rather than a general description of an event or quality. The surrounding passage determines what is being said about God in each verse.

e.t: Josedech is a personal name, rendered “Josedech” in the Hebrew Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs eight times, appearing in genealogical records and in passages connected with prophetic speech. Its role is therefore primarily identifying a person within Israel’s history, and its precise significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

This Hebrew word refers to “camels,” the animals named in two passages in Esther. It functions as a concrete noun, identifying the animals used in the royal dispatch described there. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Esther 8:10 and Esther 8:14. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: it identifies camels rather than an abstract idea, person, action, or quality. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the specific role these animals play in either passage.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 2:44, and the English rendering is “Jorkeam.” Its setting is a genealogy, where the name functions as an individual identified within a family line. No broader lexical sense is established for the name here.

The word occurs 196 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its basic meaning is well established across many passages. Its exact significance in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a ram rather than sheep in general.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “espousals,” the formal relationship in which a man and woman are pledged toward marriage. It functions as a noun, naming that covenantal marital bond rather than describing an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 2:2, so its normal meaning is especially tied to this single scriptural use. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there; the word itself identifies the espousal relationship.

This Hebrew word refers to “study,” describing that activity in its one recorded Old Testament occurrence. It appears in Ecclesiastes 12:12. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be explained beyond this basic sense. The word therefore identifies study as the activity being referred to, without enough usage evidence to establish a wider range of meanings.

“Take” is the central meaning of this Hebrew verb. It expresses an action in which a person, group, or thing is taken, and it functions as a verb within Old Testament sentences. The word occurs 121 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is used across a broad range of passages rather than belonging to one narrowly defined situation. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being taken and the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to food, often specifically meat. It describes something provided or available for nourishment, with English renderings showing both “food” and “meat.” It occurs 18 times in the Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel, so its basic sense is not limited to one passage or setting. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on food generally or on meat more specifically. References include Genesis 1:29–30, Genesis 9:3, Leviticus 11:39, and Leviticus 25:6.

Maharai is a personal name, rendered as “Maharai.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in 2 Samuel and twice in 1 Chronicles. The available passages preserve it consistently as “Maharai,” so its ordinary lexical function is simply to designate a person. The specific individual’s role or significance must be understood from the surrounding verse and passage.

Its scriptural uses concern movement, pursuit, escape, and control of access, so the word can describe a strategically important crossing point. This Hebrew word occurs 11 times in the Old Testament, from Genesis through Jeremiah. Its central idea remains a physical place of passage rather than the act of crossing itself.

Its recorded setting is a genealogy, where the name identifies a person connected with the listed family relationships. Scripture does not provide an explicit definition or translated meaning for this name.

e.t: “Elisha” is a personal name, referring to the individual known by that name rather than describing a general quality, action, or object. It functions as a proper name in the Hebrew Old Testament. This name appears 58 times in the Hebrew corpus, beginning in 1 Kings and occurring most often throughout 2 Kings. The surrounding passages repeatedly identify Elisha in speech, relationships, and significant events, but the name itself simply identifies him. Its specific significance in any particular verse depends on that passage’s context.

This Hebrew word means “bitter.” It functions as a describing word, identifying something as bitter in quality or taste. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Deuteronomy and Job. Its uses include descriptions connected with what is written, experienced, or taken in, but the surrounding verse is needed to explain each specific use. The central idea remains a sharp, unpleasant bitterness rather than a broad list of separate meanings.

The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 2 Samuel 13:9. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is straightforward: a pan. The word is connected there with speech-related scriptural material, while remaining a concrete object within the sentence.

e.t: Eleazar is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action or quality. In the Old Testament, it identifies people in Israel’s history, including a prominent priestly figure and others connected with priestly and genealogical records. The name appears 72 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Exodus through Nehemiah. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, since the same name can identify different individuals.

This Hebrew noun means “princes,” identifying people who hold an elevated place among others. It appears 29 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 26 verses. The word describes a person or group regarded as socially prominent, rather than an action or object. Its use extends across historical, poetic, and prophetic passages, showing a normal meaning associated with persons of elevated standing. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “goods,” designating material possessions or resources. It functions as a term for what can be counted, assigned, or handled as part of an official provision or financial matter. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezra, at Ezra 6:8 and Ezra 7:26. Its basic sense is therefore concrete and practical: goods viewed as something belonging to a person or available for an appointed purpose.

Nimrah is a Hebrew proper name, used as the name of a place rather than as a general descriptive word. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 32:3, and is rendered “Nimrah” in the available English renderings. Because it functions as a place-name, its meaning is primarily identification: it names a specific location. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that location’s role in the account.

This Hebrew word means “merchandise,” naming something connected with trade or commerce. It functions as a noun: it identifies merchandise rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word occurs four times in the Old Testament, appearing in Proverbs and Isaiah. Its usage therefore points to merchandise as a recognized object of economic activity, while the surrounding verse determines the specific role it has in each passage.

Saph is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Saph.” It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general concept. In the Hebrew Old Testament data here, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 21:18, so its meaning is chiefly identifying rather than descriptive. The available rendering preserves it as a name, and no explicit definition is provided. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word expresses love or describes something as lovely. It presents the idea of attractiveness or affection rather than an action, and its exact role depends on the sentence in which it appears. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel 33. The word is rendered with the meaning "love" in one occurrence and "lovely" in the other, showing that it can express either the affection itself or the quality that draws affection.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “testimony”—a witness, declaration, or enduring reminder that something has been stated or established. It commonly refers to the testimony associated with the covenant, including the tablets and the sacred chest that contained them. The word occurs 59 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Exodus, Psalms, and Numbers, and can function as something given, spoken about, guarded, or made. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “standing.” It functions as a noun, naming the state or act of standing rather than describing a person, place, or action by itself. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Micah 1:11. Because it appears only once and the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence depends on the passage’s context.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “neighbour.” It functions as a noun for another person considered in relation to oneself, especially in instructions concerning honesty, fairness, and treatment of others. It appears twelve times in the Hebrew Old Testament, most often in Leviticus and once in Zechariah. Its use presents the neighbour as someone toward whom a person has moral responsibilities, including truthful dealings and impartial judgment.

This Hebrew verb means “afflict.” It describes an action in which one person or group acts upon another, rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs 82 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it is used across many passages and settings. Its normal sense remains focused on the act of afflicting; the surrounding verse determines who acts and who receives that action.

This Hebrew word describes someone who is “childless,” referring to the absence of children. It is used four times in the Old Testament, and each recorded occurrence carries this same basic sense. The word appears in passages concerning individuals or families whose line has no child, so its focus is family continuation rather than a general condition of loneliness or poverty. The surrounding passage determines the precise force in each verse, but the ordinary meaning remains clear: having no children.

This Hebrew verb means “fear.” It describes the presence or experience of fear, especially when people face danger, opposition, or something overwhelming. It can function as the action or condition expressed about a person or people, and its uses include direct commands not to fear. The word occurs 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with several uses in Deuteronomy and Isaiah. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word is the personal name “Potiphar,” identifying a particular man rather than describing a general quality or action. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, both times in Genesis: Genesis 37:36 and Genesis 39:1. The repeated rendering “Potiphar” indicates that the word functions as a proper name. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic role is to identify this person.

This Hebrew word means “plain,” referring to a named or described place rather than an action or quality. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, with both occurrences in Judges 11:33. The available wording supports the basic sense of a plain, while the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is therefore best understood as a place-related noun meaning “plain.”

Peninnah is a personal name, referring to a particular woman rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in two verses in 1 Samuel 1. The name is consistently rendered “Peninnah,” so its ordinary function is to identify this individual. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a name, not as a description to be translated into another common noun.

The Hebrew word means “fruitful.” It functions as a verb, expressing the action or condition of being fruitful rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs 29 times, appearing from Genesis through Ezekiel. The word is used across several Old Testament books, so its basic sense is broad rather than limited to one passage or setting. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew noun means “interpretation”: an explanation that makes the meaning of something understood. It refers to the act or result of making sense of a matter, rather than to the matter itself. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ecclesiastes 8:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is an interpretation or explanation that brings understanding to what is being considered.

This Hebrew word means “tingle,” describing a prickling or intensely stirred sensation. It functions as a verb, expressing what happens when someone experiences this bodily or inward response. It occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 3:11, 2 Kings 21:12, Jeremiah 19:3, and Habakkuk 3:16. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “cockatrice,” naming a creature associated with danger. It occurs five times in the Old Testament, in Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. In Isaiah, the word appears in relationships describing the creature as something acted upon or encountered, while another recorded connection associates it with death. These patterns support understanding it as a threatening creature rather than a person, action, or abstract idea. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word refers to something named in Isaiah 54:12, but its precise English meaning cannot be determined from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, so there is no wider pattern of usage to clarify its sense. Its meaning must therefore be understood from the wording and context of Isaiah 54:12 rather than from a broader biblical usage pattern.

Kitron functions as a proper place name, identifying a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Judges 1:30, and is preserved in English as “Kitron.” Because no broader lexical definition is available, its ordinary meaning is the name of that location. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the place’s particular role in that passage.

This Hebrew word describes something cut or shorn. It appears twice in the Old Testament, with the approved meanings “cut” and “shorn.” Its basic idea concerns removing or shortening something by cutting. The word occurs once in 2 Kings 6:6 and once in Song of Songs 4:2, showing its use in more than one setting while retaining this central sense.

This Hebrew word refers to beholding—looking at or observing something. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ecclesiastes 5:11, so its ordinary meaning is supported by a single biblical use. As a noun-like expression connected with seeing, it points to the act or experience of looking rather than to a person or object itself. The exact force of the word in Ecclesiastes depends on the surrounding verse, but “beholding” clearly identifies its basic sense.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to inner disturbance or intense distress, expressed by the approved meanings “trouble” and “rage.” It can describe the painful unrest associated with human life, as well as forceful agitation or fury. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Job, where it is connected with the hardships and unrest of earthly existence. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Hebrew word refers to “vails,” naming a physical covering rather than an action or quality. It appears twice in the Old Testament, once in Song of Solomon and once in Isaiah. In both occurrences, it functions as the name of an item that can be mentioned among personal or household articles. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense is a tangible covering called “vails.”

e.t: Arieh is a personal name, functioning as the designation of a person rather than as a description or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 15:25, and the English rendering is “Arieh.” Its role is therefore to identify an individual in the passage. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific actions or significance; the word itself primarily supplies the person’s name.

e.t: This Hebrew word is a personal name, referring to Rapha in the Old Testament genealogical records. It occurs twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 8, where it identifies a person within a family line. In one occurrence, the name is connected with a birth or begetting relationship, confirming its role as an individual’s name rather than a description of an action or quality. Its precise significance beyond the name itself is not stated by the available wording.

e.t: This word is the personal name “Saul.” It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it identifies people in genealogical records and narrative accounts, including the Saul prominent in 1 Samuel. The name occurs 401 times in the Hebrew corpus, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the person and surrounding context being described.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a cry or urgent appeal, especially one directed toward God or raised in distress. Its scriptural use connects it with calling and with situations marked by severe suffering or death. It occurs eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, including passages in Exodus, Samuel, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Lamentations. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on the appeal itself or the distress behind it.

This word refers to “understanding”—the ability to grasp, recognize, or discern something. It describes inward comprehension rather than merely hearing or observing. In its three Old Testament occurrences, all in Daniel 5, it is rendered “understanding.” Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains clear: having insight that enables a person to comprehend what is being communicated or considered.

Shamlai is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, in Ezra 2:46, and the English rendering preserves it as “Shamlai.” Because the available passage information does not provide a lexical definition or the name’s meaning, it is best understood simply as the name of the person listed there. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “lips,” the visible part of the face associated with speaking and expression. It is a noun used five times in the Hebrew Scriptures. Its occurrences show the word applied to a person’s lips as an identifiable physical feature, including references connected with speech, mourning, or outward appearance. The surrounding passage determines the particular emphasis, but the ordinary sense remains the lips themselves.

This Hebrew verb means “sink.” It describes the action or result of something going downward or beneath the surface. In the Old Testament, it occurs six times, including descriptions involving waters, the sea, and things going down. Its wording can therefore express a physical descent or a lowering effect, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise application. The term appears from Numbers through Amos, showing this sense across several biblical settings.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the place name “Tabor.” It identifies a specific location rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Old Testament, it appears ten times, including references in Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, and Hosea. Its use in commands, speeches, and descriptions shows that it names a recognized place within Israel’s story. The precise significance of Tabor in any particular passage comes from that passage’s surrounding text.

e.t: This word refers to a place named “Eshtemoa,” functioning as a proper place-name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It identifies a location associated with Judah and appears six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including references in Joshua, 1 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its role is therefore to name a geographic place in the biblical record, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular information being stated about it.

This Hebrew word means “ninth,” referring to the position that follows eight in an ordered series. It functions as an ordinal number, marking a person, group, time, or other item as ninth rather than describing a quality or action. In the Old Testament, it occurs 18 times across 17 verses, including references to the ninth month, the ninth group of priests, and the ninth year or day. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the item or time period that it identifies.
